subject: D639D12CD679E3ED02A0F7A8D7835DB2
introduction: Most of what is read here was written to one person about one matter: whether to travel and by which road, where to stay and for how long, what to study, whom to marry, how to treat a patient, when to speak and when to keep a thing hidden, and why no letter has come. The hundred readings kept from the guide are set beside a hundred from elsewhere, and the nearest kin to such counsel proved to be other letters and other particular instructions: Paul asking for his cloak and his books and telling a young friend to look after his stomach, Jacob sending his sons in by different gates, Nehemiah asking leave to travel, Confucius urging one pupil forward and holding another back. Proverbs, the Preacher and the Qur’an supply the general wisdom that such counsel applies. A smaller number of voices, among them Kant, Emerson, Seneca and Rossetti, ask whether a person ought to be told so much, or to remember so faithfully. Read together they raise a question the guide leaves open for the reader: what in advice given to one life belongs to every life.
questions: Many of these instructions are particular to a person, a city and a season. What would you need to know before taking one of them as counsel for yourself?
Paul tells Timothy to take a little wine for his stomach, and the guide tells a physician to use gentle remedies. Why might care for small bodily and practical matters belong in a spiritual letter?
Several readings counsel wisdom, caution and concealment, while Jesus tells his followers to let their light shine. How do you tell when discretion protects something and when it merely hides it?
Some correspondents are told where to go, and others are told that the choice is theirs. Which do you find harder to receive, and why?
Kant calls it tutelage to rely on another's direction. In what ways does asking for guidance differ from giving up one's own judgement?
The letters ask again and again for news and for remembrance. What does keeping up a correspondence do for the one who writes and the one who waits?

outside.why: Ruth would not be parted from the one she followed: where thou goest I will go, and where thou lodgest I will lodge.
Moses asks that the words be taught to one's own children and spoken of in the house, at lying down and at rising up.
The emperor also begins with getting up in the morning, and rises to the work of a human being. Is a loving face turned to the household part of that work?
Jacob sends his sons into the city by different gates, not together, and adds that the decision rests with God alone. When is it wiser to travel apart?
Paul breaks off a solemn charge to give a young friend plain advice about his stomach and his frequent illnesses.
Rebekah's family does not settle the journey for her; they call her and ask, and she answers for herself.
James does not forbid plans to go to a city, trade there and gain; he asks that they be made with the words 'if the Lord will'. Does that change the plan or the planner?
Carlyle's rule for anyone unsure where duty lies is to do the nearest one that is known to be a duty.
Paul goes on toward Jerusalem not knowing what will befall him there, and says that none of these things move him.
Paul chooses Timothy as his messenger because he has served beside him as a son serves with his father.
Proverbs begins a child's schooling at home, with a father's instruction and a mother's law worn like an ornament.
The Samaritan's remedies are the mild ones of the road: oil and wine poured in, wounds bound up, and a beast to ride.
Proverbs counts a merry heart among the medicines. Does a physician's gentleness belong to the remedy, or only to the manner of giving it?
Paul is told in a vision by night to stay and keep speaking, and he remains there a year and six months.
The proverb's prudent man sees the evil coming and hides himself, while the simple pass on and are punished.
The commandment sets father and mother side by side as those to be honoured, and ties long days in the land to it.
The Qur'an sets kindness to parents next to the worship of God, and asks for humility and mercy toward them in their old age.
Genesis has a man leave his father and his mother to cleave to his wife. How do a mother's rights and a new household's claims sit together?
Isaiah's picture of not forgetting is a mother with her nursing child, and the promise goes further than even she can.
Paul asks the same of a young teacher: to be an example in word, in conduct, in charity, in faith and in purity.
The proverb promises the one who is diligent in his business a place before kings and not before mean men.
Seneca tells his friend that crowds are the thing most to be avoided, since he cannot yet trust himself to them safely. Is a public post a danger to character or a chance to use it?
Paul's advice is close to this: study to be quiet, do your own business, work with your own hands, and walk honestly.
Those whom Jesus sends out travel light: no purse, no bag, no shoes, and no greetings to delay them on the road.
The builder in the parable sits down first and counts the cost, to see whether there is enough to finish the tower.
Proverbs gives the householder the same plain charge: know the state of your flocks and look well to your herds.
Bacon's sentence divides such a training in three: reading for fullness, conference for readiness, and writing for exactness.
Kant calls it tutelage to be unable to use one's understanding without direction from another. Is asking a trusted teacher what to study a want of courage, or a use of judgement?
The Preacher's counsel for any task is to do whatever the hand finds to do with all one's might.
Sow in the morning and do not hold back the hand in the evening, says the Preacher, since no one knows which will prosper.
Paul tells Timothy to give himself to reading, exhortation and doctrine, and not to neglect the gift that is in him.
Paul sends Onesimus back to Philemon as a brother beloved, and asks him as a partner to receive him as he would Paul himself.
Emerson would have every heart trust itself. When a choice is handed back with the words 'the choice is yours', is that trust in a person or a test of them?
Paul ends with the same charge: be steadfast, unmoveable, always abounding in the work, because the labour is not in vain.
Paul's company is twice kept from the places they meant to go, and then called in a vision to come over into Macedonia.
The healed man asks to go with Jesus and is sent home instead, to tell his own friends what has been done for him.
Paul puts off a visit and stays at Ephesus until Pentecost, because a great door has opened to him there, with many adversaries.
Abram is sent out with no route at all, only toward a land that will be shown him. Which asks more trust, an itinerary of named cities or none?
Paul's directions to Titus are as particular: come to Nicopolis, where he has decided to winter, and bring two travellers on their way.
Joseph is told where to take the child and his mother and to stay there until he is brought word.
Nehemiah asks the king's leave to travel, prays even as he asks, and is sent once he has set a time for his return.
The Qur'an joins the same two things: call to the way of the Lord with wisdom and fair exhortation, and reason in the better way.
Mary's way with what she had heard and seen was to keep all of it and ponder it in her heart.
The proverb holds both halves together: a person's heart devises the way, and the Lord directs the steps.
Polonius hands his son back to himself: be true to your own self. Is being left free to choose one's direction a lighter instruction or a heavier one?
Paul proposes going back to every city where they had preached the word, to see how the brethren there are doing.
Paul describes his own manner among those he visited: gentle, as a nurse cherishes her children, and affectionately desirous of them.
The elder too will not put everything into ink, and trusts instead to see his friend shortly and speak face to face.
Paul plans a route as well: long hindered, he will see the Romans on his journey into Spain and be brought on his way by them.
Confucius would keep a son from going far while his parents live, or at least have him name a fixed place. Whose claim does a long journey of service set aside?
Sheep sent out among wolves are told to be wise as serpents and harmless as doves, both at once.
Proverbs puts it in a line: the prudent conceal what they know, and the heart of fools proclaims foolishness.
The Qur'an forbids taking unbelievers as friends in preference to believers, except where the faithful are guarding themselves against them.
Jesus tells his followers to let their light shine before others so that their good works are seen. When is concealment the faithful course, and for how long?
Jesus gives a reason for withholding what is holy: it will be trampled under foot, and the tramplers will turn on the giver.
The healed man is charged to say nothing and publishes it everywhere, until Jesus can no longer enter the city openly. What does a broken silence cost the one who asked for it?
Paul's letter of introduction for Phebe asks the same: receive her as is fitting and assist her in whatever she needs.
Paul also trusts his news to a carrier: Tychicus, a faithful minister, will make known in person everything that is done.
Jesus spoke the word to the crowd as they were able to hear it, and expounded all things to his disciples when they were alone.
Paul's invitation to Timothy is as short and as pressing: do thy diligence to come before winter.
Paul also had to account for a changed itinerary, and to deny that he had planned lightly, with yes and no together.
Jesus puts off a request with the same kind of reason, saying that his hour is not yet come.
Paul knows the other side of waiting: he longs to see the Romans, has often purposed to come, and has been prevented until now.
The Qur'an lets the sick and the traveller fast on other days, and says that God desires ease for them and not hardship.
Paul lists his own journeys as perils of waters, of robbers and of his own countrymen. Is care for one's health a condition of service or a limit on it?
Paul writes of being parted from friends in presence but not in heart, and of his great desire to see their face.
Paul's summons has the same urgency and the same detail: come shortly, and bring Mark with you, for he is profitable for the ministry.
Longfellow's stanza refuses delay in the same spirit: trust no future, let the dead past bury its dead, act in the living present.
Proverbs expects such a decision to be asked about: purposes are disappointed without counsel and established among many counsellors.
Confucius explains why he urged one pupil forward and kept another back: one was retiring and slow, the other had energy to spare. Should advice fit the question or the person asking?
Paul's letters were passed on too: this one to be read at Laodicea, and the epistle from Laodicea to be read in turn.
Paul's letters carry the same remembrance of his friends: thanks at every thought of them and a request for them in every prayer.
Proverbs knows what a letter is worth: good news from a far country is like cold waters to a thirsty soul.
Lincoln begins a letter by admitting how weak and fruitless any words of his must be. What does a letter give, beyond its words, when the writer is pressed and far away?
Jethro tells Moses that the thing is too heavy for him alone and that he will surely wear away. How does a guide stay open to each person without being consumed?
Paul calls his friends themselves his epistle, written in the heart and read by everyone. What can a life say that the busiest pen cannot?
Rossetti's speaker releases the one left behind: better to forget and smile than to remember and be sad. Is 'forget me not' a burden laid on a friend or a gift to them?
Donne tells the one he is leaving that two souls which are one suffer no breach by parting, only an expansion.
Paul remembers Timothy night and day, is mindful of his tears, and greatly desires to see him and be filled with joy.
Proverbs gives a reason why friends need each other's news and company: iron sharpens iron, and a friend sharpens a friend.
The Qur'an's own instruction for recitation is also about quantity and pace: add a little, and chant in measure.
Bacon would have a reader neither contradict nor take for granted, but weigh and consider. What does reading one verse a hundred times do that weighing it once cannot?
The psalmist keeps the word in the same place, hidden in the heart, so as not to sin against God.
Joshua is told that the book of the law is not to leave his mouth, and to meditate in it day and night.
John's book opens with a blessing on the one who reads, on those who hear, and on those who keep what is written.
Philip asks a reader whether he understands what he reads, and the man answers that he needs someone to guide him. Is hearing a call in a text something a reader does alone?
Hosea's God speaks of the same long rearing: teaching a child to walk, healing unnoticed, and drawing with bands of love.
The psalmist's complaint has the same opening words: how long wilt thou forget me, how long hide thy face from me?
The Qur'an's command about trust is concrete: restore what is deposited with you to its owners, and judge justly.
Jesus measures trustworthiness from the small end: whoever is faithful in what is least is faithful also in much.
Paul's charge to Timothy is to keep what has been committed to his trust and to avoid profane and vain babblings.
The Stoic picture of holding one's station is a promontory on which the waves keep breaking while it stands firm.
The elder writes the same wish to a friend far away: that he may prosper and be in health, as his soul prospers.
In the parable a man travelling to a far country delivers his goods to his own servants, to each according to his ability.
The Qur'an promises the steadfast their wages without stint, and reminds the believers that God's earth is spacious.
The Stoic's steadiness comes from wishing things to happen as they do happen. Is steadfastness in a cause the same calm, or does it want something to change?
The psalm hears the promise from the other side: I will instruct thee, teach thee the way to go, and guide thee with mine eye.
Jesus says the same of those he sends: whoever receives them receives him, and the one who sent him.
Polonius advises reserve of the same kind: give every man your ear but few your voice, and keep your judgement to yourself.
The Preacher gives silence and speech each its own time. How does a reader tell which time it is for what has been entrusted to them?

timothy-the-cloke-and-the-books.text: The cloke that I left at Troas with Carpus, when thou comest, bring with thee, and the books, but especially the parchments

timothy-a-little-wine.text: Drink no longer water, but use a little wine for thy stomach's sake and thine often infirmities

proverbs-direct-thy-paths.text: In all thy ways acknowledge him, and he shall direct thy paths

psalm-instruct-thee-and-teach-thee.text: I will instruct thee and teach thee in the way which thou shalt go: I will guide thee with mine eye

james-if-the-lord-will.text: Go to now, ye that say, To day or to morrow we will go into such a city, and continue there a year, and buy and sell, and get gain: Whereas ye know not what shall be on the morrow. For what is your life? It is even a vapour, that appeareth for a little time, and then vanisheth away. For that ye ought to say, If the Lord will, we shall live, and do this, or that

acts-come-over-into-macedonia.text: Now when they had gone throughout Phrygia and the region of Galatia, and were forbidden of the Holy Ghost to preach the word in Asia, After they were come to Mysia, they assayed to go into Bithynia: but the Spirit suffered them not. And they passing by Mysia came down to Troas. And a vision appeared to Paul in the night; There stood a man of Macedonia, and prayed him, saying, Come over into Macedonia, and help us. And after he had seen the vision, immediately we endeavoured to go into Macedonia, assuredly gathering that the Lord had called us for to preach the gospel unto them

acts-much-people-in-this-city.text: Then spake the Lord to Paul in the night by a vision, Be not afraid, but speak, and hold not thy peace: For I am with thee, and no man shall set on thee to hurt thee: for I have much people in this city. And he continued there a year and six months, teaching the word of God among them

corinthians-abide-in-the-same-calling.text: Let every man abide in the same calling wherein he was called

thessalonians-study-to-be-quiet.text: And that ye study to be quiet, and to do your own business, and to work with your own hands, as we commanded you; That ye may walk honestly toward them that are without, and that ye may have lack of nothing

luke-carry-neither-purse.text: Go your ways: behold, I send you forth as lambs among wolves. Carry neither purse, nor scrip, nor shoes: and salute no man by the way. And into whatsoever house ye enter, first say, Peace be to this house. And if the son of peace be there, your peace shall rest upon it: if not, it shall turn to you again. And in the same house remain, eating and drinking such things as they give: for the labourer is worthy of his hire. Go not from house to house

proverbs-without-counsel.text: Without counsel purposes are disappointed: but in the multitude of counsellors they are established

titus-be-diligent-to-come.text: When I shall send Artemas unto thee, or Tychicus, be diligent to come unto me to Nicopolis: for I have determined there to winter. Bring Zenas the lawyer and Apollos on their journey diligently, that nothing be wanting unto them. And let our's also learn to maintain good works for necessary uses, that they be not unfruitful

philemon-receive-him.text: For perhaps he therefore departed for a season, that thou shouldest receive him for ever; Not now as a servant, but above a servant, a brother beloved, specially to me, but how much more unto thee, both in the flesh, and in the Lord? If thou count me therefore a partner, receive him as myself

romans-phebe-our-sister.text: I commend unto you Phebe our sister, which is a servant of the church which is at Cenchrea: That ye receive her in the Lord, as becometh saints, and that ye assist her in whatsoever business she hath need of you: for she hath been a succourer of many, and of myself also

timothy-neglect-not-the-gift.text: Till I come, give attendance to reading, to exhortation, to doctrine. Neglect not the gift that is in thee, which was given thee by prophecy, with the laying on of the hands of the presbytery. Meditate upon these things; give thyself wholly to them; that thy profiting may appear to all. Take heed unto thyself, and unto the doctrine; continue in them: for in doing this thou shalt both save thyself, and them that hear thee

proverbs-heart-deviseth-his-way.text: A man's heart deviseth his way: but the Lord directeth his steps

quran-luqman-o-my-dear-son.text: O my dear son! Establish worship and enjoin kindness and forbid iniquity, and persevere whatever may befall thee. Lo! that is of the steadfast heart of things. Turn not thy cheek in scorn toward folk, nor walk with pertness in the land. Lo! Allah loveth not each braggart boaster. Be modest in thy bearing and subdue thy voice. Lo! the harshest of all voices is the voice of the ass

quran-lower-the-wing-of-submission.text: Thy Lord hath decreed, that ye worship none save Him, and (that ye show) kindness to parents. If one of them or both of them attain old age with thee, say not "Fie" unto them nor repulse them, but speak unto them a gracious word. And lower unto them the wing of submission through mercy, and say: My Lord! Have mercy on them both as they did care for me when I was little

analects-yu-and-chiu.text: Ch'iu is retiring and slow; therefore I urged him forward. Yu has more than his own share of energy; therefore I kept him back
analects-yu-and-chiu.author: Confucius

romans-i-long-to-see-you.text: For I long to see you, that I may impart unto you some spiritual gift, to the end ye may be established; That is, that I may be comforted together with you by the mutual faith both of you and me. Now I would not have you ignorant, brethren, that oftentimes I purposed to come unto you, (but was let hitherto,) that I might have some fruit among you also, even as among other Gentiles

romans-my-journey-into-spain.text: For which cause also I have been much hindered from coming to you. But now having no more place in these parts, and having a great desire these many years to come unto you; Whensoever I take my journey into Spain, I will come to you: for I trust to see you in my journey, and to be brought on my way thitherward by you, if first I be somewhat filled with your company

corinthians-a-great-door-and-effectual.text: Now I will come unto you, when I shall pass through Macedonia: for I do pass through Macedonia. And it may be that I will abide, yea, and winter with you, that ye may bring me on my journey whithersoever I go. For I will not see you now by the way; but I trust to tarry a while with you, if the Lord permit. But I will tarry at Ephesus until Pentecost. For a great door and effectual is opened unto me, and there are many adversaries

philippians-no-man-likeminded.text: But I trust in the Lord Jesus to send Timotheus shortly unto you, that I also may be of good comfort, when I know your state. For I have no man likeminded, who will naturally care for your state. For all seek their own, not the things which are Jesus Christ's. But ye know the proof of him, that, as a son with the father, he hath served with me in the gospel

timothy-thy-grandmother-lois.text: I thank God, whom I serve from my forefathers with pure conscience, that without ceasing I have remembrance of thee in my prayers night and day; Greatly desiring to see thee, being mindful of thy tears, that I may be filled with joy; When I call to remembrance the unfeigned faith that is in thee, which dwelt first in thy grandmother Lois, and thy mother Eunice; and I am persuaded that in thee also

timothy-only-luke-is-with-me.text: Do thy diligence to come shortly unto me: For Demas hath forsaken me, having loved this present world, and is departed unto Thessalonica; Crescens to Galatia, Titus unto Dalmatia. Only Luke is with me. Take Mark, and bring him with thee: for he is profitable to me for the ministry

timothy-come-before-winter.text: Do thy diligence to come before winter

timothy-keep-that-which-is-committed.text: O Timothy, keep that which is committed to thy trust, avoiding profane and vain babblings, and oppositions of science falsely so called

mark-go-home-to-thy-friends.text: And when he was come into the ship, he that had been possessed with the devil prayed him that he might be with him. Howbeit Jesus suffered him not, but saith unto him, Go home to thy friends, and tell them how great things the Lord hath done for thee, and hath had compassion on thee

mark-say-nothing-to-any-man.text: And he straitly charged him, and forthwith sent him away; And saith unto him, See thou say nothing to any man: but go thy way, shew thyself to the priest, and offer for thy cleansing those things which Moses commanded, for a testimony unto them. But he went out, and began to publish it much, and to blaze abroad the matter, insomuch that Jesus could no more openly enter into the city, but was without in desert places: and they came to him from every quarter

acts-the-will-of-the-lord-be-done.text: And when we heard these things, both we, and they of that place, besought him not to go up to Jerusalem. Then Paul answered, What mean ye to weep and to break mine heart? for I am ready not to be bound only, but also to die at Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus. And when he would not be persuaded, we ceased, saying, The will of the Lord be done

exodus-jethro-not-good.text: And Moses' father in law said unto him, The thing that thou doest is not good. Thou wilt surely wear away, both thou, and this people that is with thee: for this thing is too heavy for thee; thou art not able to perform it thyself alone. Hearken now unto my voice, I will give thee counsel, and God shall be with thee: Be thou for the people to God-ward, that thou mayest bring the causes unto God

colossians-tychicus-declare.text: All my state shall Tychicus declare unto you, who is a beloved brother, and a faithful minister and fellowservant in the Lord: Whom I have sent unto you for the same purpose, that he might know your estate, and comfort your hearts; With Onesimus, a faithful and beloved brother, who is one of you. They shall make known unto you all things which are done here

colossians-read-among-you.text: And when this epistle is read among you, cause that it be read also in the church of the Laodiceans; and that ye likewise read the epistle from Laodicea

revelation-blessed-is-he-that-readeth.text: Blessed is he that readeth, and they that hear the words of this prophecy, and keep those things which are written therein: for the time is at hand

luke-mary-kept-all-these-things.text: But Mary kept all these things, and pondered them in her heart

proverbs-talebearer-revealeth-secrets.text: A talebearer revealeth secrets: but he that is of a faithful spirit concealeth the matter

proverbs-prudent-man-concealeth.text: A prudent man concealeth knowledge: but the heart of fools proclaimeth foolishness

proverbs-state-of-thy-flocks.text: Be thou diligent to know the state of thy flocks, and look well to thy herds

nehemiah-i-set-him-a-time.text: Then the king said unto me, For what dost thou make request? So I prayed to the God of heaven. And I said unto the king, If it please the king, and if thy servant have found favour in thy sight, that thou wouldest send me unto Judah, unto the city of my fathers' sepulchres, that I may build it. And the king said unto me, (the queen also sitting by him,) For how long shall thy journey be? and when wilt thou return? So it pleased the king to send me; and I set him a time

genesis-i-will-go.text: And they called Rebekah, and said unto her, Wilt thou go with this man? And she said, I will go

corinthians-yea-and-nay.text: And in this confidence I was minded to come unto you before, that ye might have a second benefit; And to pass by you into Macedonia, and to come again out of Macedonia unto you, and of you to be brought on my way toward Judaea. When I therefore was thus minded, did I use lightness? or the things that I purpose, do I purpose according to the flesh, that with me there should be yea yea, and nay nay

acts-let-us-go-again.text: And some days after Paul said unto Barnabas, Let us go again and visit our brethren in every city where we have preached the word of the Lord, and see how they do

quran-enter-by-different-gates.text: And he said: O my sons! Go not in by one gate; go in by different gates. I can naught avail you as against Allah. Lo! the decision rests with Allah only. In Him do I put my trust, and in Him let all the trusting put their trust.

quran-the-chiefs-take-counsel.text: And a man came from the uttermost part of the city, running. He said: O Moses! Lo! the chiefs take counsel against thee to slay thee; therefor escape. Lo! I am of those who give thee good advice.

quran-guard-yourselves-against-them.text: Let not the believers take disbelievers for their friends in preference to believers. Whoso doeth that hath no connection with Allah unless (it be) that ye but guard yourselves against them, taking (as it were) security. Allah biddeth you beware (only) of Himself. Unto Allah is the journeying.

analects-not-go-abroad.text: While his parents are alive, the son may not go abroad to a distance. If he does go abroad, he must have a fixed place to which he goes
analects-not-go-abroad.author: Confucius
